stem:
A 26-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes asks why his muscles and fat cannot use blood glucose without insulin injections, yet his brain continues to function.

Which of the following best explains this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Muscle cells prefer fatty acids, so they ignore circulating glucose entirely
options.misconception: A starvation adaptation is being treated as the reason uptake fails.
options.explanation: Muscle is insulin's primary target for glucose uptake; without insulin the transporter-mediated uptake fails even though glucose is abundant — the tissue is not simply choosing fat.

options.label: B
options.text: Muscle and fat need insulin for glucose uptake; brain cells do not
options.misconception: None; skeletal muscle and adipose cells are insulin's primary targets, while brain and several other tissues are insulin-independent.
options.explanation: Insulin facilitates glucose uptake into body cells, with skeletal muscle and adipose cells as primary targets; red blood cells and cells of the brain, liver, kidneys, and small intestinal lining lack insulin receptors and take up glucose without it.

options.label: C
options.text: Brain cells convert amino acids to glucose inside the cell
options.misconception: A biosynthetic pathway is being invented to explain insulin independence.
options.explanation: The brain takes glucose directly from blood without requiring insulin because its cells lack insulin receptors; no internal synthesis explains the difference.

options.label: D
options.text: Fat cells store glucose as glycogen without any hormonal signal
options.misconception: The wrong tissue is being described as insulin-independent.
options.explanation: Adipose cells are primary insulin targets and need insulin for glucose uptake; the insulin-independent tissues are red blood cells, brain, liver, kidney, and intestinal lining cells.

options.label: E
options.text: Insulin acts mainly by suppressing glucagon rather than on peripheral tissues
options.misconception: An indirect effect is being substituted for insulin's primary action.
options.explanation: Insulin's primary function is facilitating glucose uptake into body cells, chiefly skeletal muscle and adipose tissue; it does far more than modulate other hormones.

context: Learning objective: define insulin's targets. Insulin (pancreatic beta cells, ~75% of each islet) is released when blood glucose rises and facilitates cellular glucose uptake; skeletal muscle and adipose cells are the primary targets, while red blood cells, brain, liver, kidney, and intestinal lining cells do not require insulin.
imageCaption: Insulin (fed, storage) vs glucagon (fast, mobilization/ketogenesis); type 1 = beta-cell loss.
